WEEK 3

Confidence Intervals

Felipe Campelo

In this lecture…

In this lecture, we’ll go over the main concepts related to quantifying our uncertainty when estimating parameters. More specifically, we will:

  • Explore the concept of a confidence intervaland its interpretation in terms of sampling variability.
  • Learn how to construct and interpret CIs for a population mean, under different assumptions (normal distribution with known and with unknown, large-sample approximate intervals).
  • See how sample size, variability, and confidence level affect the width / precision of the interval.

Motivation

Last week we discussed concepts related to point estimation of parameters –that is, given a sample, how to get the best possible estimateof the true value of a populational parameter. However, given that point estimates are subject to sampling variability, we know that they will almost always be a bit “off-target”.

We also saw how we can use standard errorsto quantify the uncertainty associated with our estimates. However, although standard errors provide a sense of how much an estimate would vary across repeated samples, it is an incomplete quantification of uncertainty.

What is commonly needed to support decision-making is a range of plausible values for the true population parameter, which captures the real value of the parameter with a known level of confidence.

Definition

Confidence intervals(CIs) quantify the degree of uncertainty associated with the estimation of population parameterssuch as the mean, variance, proportion, difference of means etc..

A CI can be defined as an interval that is expected to contain the true value of a given population parameter with a confidence level of ;

A useful way to think about confidence intervals in terms of confidence in the method: The method used to derive the interval has a hit rate of - i.e., the interval generated has a chance of having captured the true value of the population parameter.

Example

Suppose that you get some data related to the daily concentration of Calcium in your local water supply. Confidence level and interval width

Notice that the confidence level is a user-defined parameter. Common choices are 0.95 (95%) or 0.99 (99%). Why don’t people go for 100% confidence?

Given a sample, the width of the confidence interval increases as we increase the desired level of confidence - i.e., there is a trade-off between the precision of the interval and its confidence level.

CI for the mean of a normal variable, unknown

If the variance of the data-generating distribution is unknown, the standard error of the mean is estimated as and we have

,

distributed according to Student’s distribution with degrees-of-freedom. The distribution is a bell-shaped distribution like the normal, but with heavier tails, meaning that the quantiles are located farther away from the centre.

A confidence interval can be calculated analogously to the previous case:

Normal vs. t distribution

For small sample sizes (= low degrees of freedom) the t-distribution is more “flattened”: heavier tails leading to more conservative (wider) intervals. For large sample sizes, the differences progressively vanish.

For smaller sample sizes, t-derived confidence intervals on the mean are wider than the known-variance ones (to account for greater uncertainty in the estimated standard deviation, ).

Large-sample CI for , any distribution.

So far, we have assumed that the data-generating distribution is normal. What happens when it is not? Recall the formula for the confidence interval on the mean of a normal variable:

Notice that the connection between the data-generating distribution and the confidence interval formula is mediated by the sample mean . Now, the CLT tells us that, for i.i.d. observations, the sampling distribution of the means converges to a normal distribution regardless of the original data distribution (as long as the mean and variance are finite and the variance is not zero).

Large-sample CI for , any distribution.

This means that, for large , the quantity has a distribution that is very close to the standard normal distribution. Consequently, we can use

to estimate the confidence interval on the mean, and the actual coverage of the interval (i.e., the proportion of times that the interval contain the actual value of the populational mean) will converge to the confidence level .

CIs for the difference of two means

One important point that we'll come back to later in the course is that we are often interested in estimating not only parameters from one specific distribution, but differences (or ratios, or sums) of the parameters of two distributions.

For instance, a very common situation in A/B testing involves comparing the mean performance of two different approaches (recall our silly example in week 1). In this case, we're interested in estimating the difference of two means and its associated confidence interval.

Example: Resting heart rate

The National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) is a large, publicly available U.S. health survey that combines questionnaires with actual physical examinations and laboratory measurements.

NHANES provides a lot of measurements of health variables for tens of thousands of participants, which makes it an interesting dataset to explore all sorts of questions.

Today, we’ll use if to check the following question: In non-smoking men aged between 40 and 50 years of age, what is the difference in the mean resting heart rate of people who do not exercise vs. those who do?

CIs for other parameters / distributions

If your data-generating process follows a known probability distribution, there are often specific formulas to calculate confidence intervals. For large sample sizes, these are often based on the approximate interval template:

For smaller sample sizes, there are distribution-specific formulas or procedures that can usually be easily found. E.g., the exact CI on the variance of a normal distribution can be calculated using:

CIs for other parameters / distributions

The more general case, in which the data-generating distribution cannot be easily described as a known / canonical random variable, requires distribution-free methods.

There are a few such methods based on sophisticated statistical results, but one of the most common (and most powerful) is called the bootstrap. This method is based on repeated resampling of the available sample and the distribution of an empirical estimate of the sampling distribution of any statistic of interest.

We will discuss the bootstrap in this week’s lab session.

In this lecture we discussed…

  • What confidence intervals represent and how they express uncertainty around sample estimates of parameters.
  • How to derive and compute confidence intervals for a population mean under different scenarios.
  • The influence of sample size, variability, and confidence level on interval width and precision.

Confidence intervals express estimation uncertainty as a range with a quantified degree of certainty, helping you make statistically sound decisions with a better awareness of the (un)certainty of your estimates.
